```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
backends <- attribute_truth_backends()
crowdkit_available <- isTRUE(backends$available[backends$backend == "crowd_kit"])
truthdiscovery_available <- isTRUE(backends$available[backends$backend == "truthdiscovery"])
```

`vignette("truth-fusion")`, `vignette("truth-fusion-crowdkit")`, and
`vignette("truth-fusion-truthdiscovery")` each demonstrate one method family
on simulated data with a known ground truth. This vignette runs all three
on something closer to what this package actually exists for: real,
de-identified output from a physician-credentialing linkage pipeline, with
**no ground truth available at all** -- exactly the situation
`attribute_truth_fusion()` and the rest of this package's no-gold-standard
family are built for (see the Design rules in `README.md`, and
`docs/validation-protocol.md` for why a real benchmark against verified
locations does not exist yet).

## Where this data comes from

The `midwifery` research project maintains an AMCB (American Midwifery
Certification Board) certificant panel, each row linked to an NPI and
cross-referenced against NPPES (the National Plan and Provider Enumeration
System) for practice location. Two separate extractions of this linkage
exist, pulled about nine years apart: one dated to NPPES practice-location
data as of 2017, the other as of 2026. Comparing practice **state** for the
10,507 certificants present in both extractions:

- 9,377 (89.25%) show the same state in both extractions.
- 1,130 (10.75%) show a **different** state.

That disagreement rate is itself informative -- it is a real, unfiltered
measure of how often a single registry's own practice-location field drifts
over nine years for actively certified clinicians -- but whose row is
right, for any given certificant, is not independently known. Nothing here
has been phone-verified or board-confirmed; both "sources" below are
ultimately NPPES-derived, just pulled nine years apart.

The sample below is a de-identified, randomly drawn 50-row excerpt (35
agreeing, 15 disagreeing, reproducing the real 70/30 oversample of the rarer
disagreement case rather than the full panel's 89/11 split, so there is
enough of the interesting case to look at) with sequential placeholder
`entity_id`s in place of real NPIs -- the state values and extraction years
themselves are real.

```{r data}
claims <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c(
    "mw_001","mw_001","mw_002","mw_002","mw_003","mw_003","mw_004","mw_004","mw_005","mw_005",
    "mw_006","mw_006","mw_007","mw_007","mw_008","mw_008","mw_009","mw_009","mw_010","mw_010",
    "mw_011","mw_011","mw_012","mw_012","mw_013","mw_013","mw_014","mw_014","mw_015","mw_015",
    "mw_016","mw_016","mw_017","mw_017","mw_018","mw_018","mw_019","mw_019","mw_020","mw_020",
    "mw_021","mw_021","mw_022","mw_022","mw_023","mw_023","mw_024","mw_024","mw_025","mw_025",
    "mw_026","mw_026","mw_027","mw_027","mw_028","mw_028","mw_029","mw_029","mw_030","mw_030",
    "mw_031","mw_031","mw_032","mw_032","mw_033","mw_033","mw_034","mw_034","mw_035","mw_035",
    "mw_036","mw_036","mw_037","mw_037","mw_038","mw_038","mw_039","mw_039","mw_040","mw_040",
    "mw_041","mw_041","mw_042","mw_042","mw_043","mw_043","mw_044","mw_044","mw_045","mw_045",
    "mw_046","mw_046","mw_047","mw_047","mw_048","mw_048","mw_049","mw_049","mw_050","mw_050"
  ),
  attribute = "practice_state",
  source_id = rep(c("nppes_2017_extract", "nppes_2026_extract"), 50),

    "CA","CA","CA","CA","HI","PA","AZ","AZ","OR","OR","MN","MN","IL","MA","NY","NY","VT","VT","NY","NY",
    "MA","RI","GA","GA","DE","DE","WY","UT","RI","RI","MA","MA","MN","MN","FL","FL","OH","OH","MN","MN",

    "NY","PA","NY","NY","NC","NC","NV","NV","WV","WV","FL","GA","LA","TX","NC","ME","ID","MT","AK","IL",

```

## Phase 1: majority vote hits its structural ceiling

```{r majority}
majority_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "majority")
majority_result
table(majority_result$predictions$abstained)
disagreeing_ids <- majority_result$predictions$entity_id[majority_result$predictions$abstained]
```

Exactly the 15 known-disagreeing certificants abstain, every one with
`abstention_reason = "tied_vote"`. This is not a weakness particular to
this dataset -- it is a mathematical property of majority voting with
**exactly two** sources: a vote between two voters either agrees
unanimously or ties. There is no three-way split, no 2-of-3 outvote, no
possible way for plain majority to ever actually resolve a genuine
disagreement here, no matter how the votes fall. With only two sources,
majority voting can tell you *that* something is contested; it cannot
tell you *which side* to believe.

## Phase 2: Dawid-Skene can break the tie -- but on what basis?

```{r dawid-skene, eval = crowdkit_available}
ds_result <- suppressWarnings(attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "dawid_skene"))
ds_result$predictions[ds_result$predictions$entity_id %in% disagreeing_ids,
                       c("entity_id", "predicted_value", "model_score", "abstained")]
```

Fourteen of the fifteen ties are resolved (one, `mw_014`, is still an exact
tie even under Dawid-Skene). Unlike majority, Dawid-Skene brings in
*prior* information -- each source's learned tendency to agree with
whichever value the other 35 certificants' evidence favors -- and that is
enough to break most of these local 1-1 deadlocks with a non-trivial
`model_score`.

**This is not evidence that Dawid-Skene picked the correct state.** Both
"sources" here are the *same underlying registry*, observed nine years
apart. Dawid-Skene has no notion of which snapshot is more recent -- it
treats `nppes_2017_extract` and `nppes_2026_extract` exactly as it would
treat two genuinely independent registries, learning a symmetric
reliability score for each from how often they happen to agree with the
eventual consensus. If one extraction is simply *newer*, that is a
**recency** fact, not a **reliability** fact, and nothing in this model
knows the difference.

## Phase 3: the TruthFinder family, same caveat

```{r truthfinder, eval = truthdiscovery_available}
sums_result <- suppressWarnings(attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "sums"))
sums_result$predictions[sums_result$predictions$entity_id %in% disagreeing_ids,
                         c("entity_id", "predicted_value", "model_score", "score_type")]
```

Same pattern, same caveat: `score_type = "uncalibrated_belief"`, not a
probability, and not validated against anything -- see
`vignette("truth-fusion-truthdiscovery")`.

## A second real example: three genuinely independent sources

The panel above only ever has two sources, and both are ultimately
NPPES-derived -- not a limitation of real data in general, just of that
particular panel. A separate, unrelated piece of the same `midwifery`
project independently needed to fuse **three** genuinely independent
federal sources -- NPPES, a combined DAC/PECOS source, and CMS Open
Payments -- for a cohort of 1,806 adjudicated physician/midwife
relocations, and wrote its own one-coin Dawid-Skene EM from scratch to do
it (`diagnose_truth_discovery_migration_states.R`, a prototype, not yet
using this package). NPPES, PECOS-derived data, and CMS Open Payments are
all federal transparency datasets, explicitly public by design -- the NPIs
below are real, not placeholders.

```{r real-multisource}
claims3 <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c(
    "1023414869","1023414869","1023414869","1043687064","1043687064","1083249650","1083249650","1083249650","1083320303","1083320303",
    "1083320303","1144628298","1144628298","1245515808","1245515808","1275805459","1275805459","1275805459","1336892694","1336892694",
    "1386039246","1386039246","1396458402","1396458402","1487917217","1487917217","1639626245","1639626245","1639626245","1710985510",
    "1710985510","1710985510","1780336768","1780336768"
  ),
  attribute = "practice_state",
  reference_year = c(
    2024,2024,2024,2023,2023,2023,2023,2023,2024,2024,
    2024,2023,2023,2023,2023,2024,2024,2024,2024,2024,
    2019,2019,2024,2024,2025,2025,2024,2024,2024,2025,
    2025,2025,2024,2024
  ),
  source_id = c(
    "nppes","open_payments","dac_pecos_combined","nppes","dac_pecos_combined","open_payments","dac_pecos_combined","nppes","dac_pecos_combined","nppes",
    "open_payments","dac_pecos_combined","nppes","dac_pecos_combined","nppes","nppes","dac_pecos_combined","open_payments","dac_pecos_combined","nppes",
    "dac_pecos_combined","nppes","dac_pecos_combined","nppes","nppes","dac_pecos_combined","open_payments","dac_pecos_combined","nppes","nppes",
    "dac_pecos_combined","open_payments","nppes","dac_pecos_combined"
  ),
  claimed_value = c(
    "WI","WI","WI","CT","ME","TX","TX","TX","AZ","AZ",
    "AZ","OK","NC","MD","AZ","DE","DE","DE","MI","WA",
    "SC","GA","NJ","PA","MI","TX","LA","LA","LA","OH",
    "OH","OH","NY","NJ"
  )
)
```

This 14-NPI, 34-claim excerpt is deliberately oversampled toward the
interesting case (8 majority-tied NPI-years, 6 three-source-unanimous
ones) out of the real cohort, the same way the panel sample above was --
it is not a representative random draw.

```{r real-multisource-majority}
majority_result3 <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims3, method = "majority")
mean(majority_result3$predictions$abstained)
```

```{r real-multisource-ds, eval = crowdkit_available}
ds_result3 <- suppressWarnings(attribute_truth_fusion(claims3, method = "dawid_skene"))
mean(ds_result3$predictions$abstained)
unique(ds_result3$source_diagnostics[, c("source_id", "reliability_score")])
```

`dawid_skene` resolves most, not all, of the 8 ties on this small excerpt,
and its learned reliability ranking here is visibly noisy -- 14 NPIs is not
enough to separate three sources' reliability cleanly. Fit the identical
model on the real, full cohort behind this excerpt (3,556 NPI-years across
1,631 real midwives) and the ranking stabilizes: `nppes` 0.881,
`open_payments` 0.712, `dac_pecos_combined` 0.644 -- consistently `nppes`
first, in both the small excerpt and the full cohort, just noisier at n=14.
At full scale, `dawid_skene` resolves 695 of the NPI-years majority could
only tie on, and in this cohort it **never** overturns a majority that
already had a decisive answer (0 cases) -- a more modest value-add than
the engineered example below, and the honest one: real data, at real
scale, mostly helps by resolving genuine ties, not by reversing confident
wrong answers.

### An external signal, still not a validated benchmark

This cohort comes with one thing the panel above doesn't: an *independent*
corroboration flag (`confirmed`), built from a same-direction-twice
stability rule over a separate adjudication script, not from anything
`attribute_truth_fusion()` sees. It is not phone-verified ground truth --
see `docs/validation-protocol.md` for why nothing in this package claims
that -- but it is evidence that doesn't come from the fusion model itself,
which is more than the simulated example below can offer. On the 941
contested NPI-years with a `confirmed`/not-`confirmed` label, `dawid_skene`'s
posterior confidence in NPPES's own claim averages **0.923** for
independently-confirmed moves versus **0.888** for unconfirmed ones; plain
majority's analogous vote share shows the same direction but a smaller
gap (0.837 vs. 0.819). A real, if modest, sign that weighting by learned
reliability tracks independent corroboration slightly better than
unweighted counting -- not dramatic, and still not an accuracy benchmark.

One more real, independently-discovered parallel: DAC and PECOS share a
documented upstream dependency (DAC's address field is CMS-derived from
PECOS enrollment directly) -- the same "shared upstream feed" setup as
`vignette("truth-fusion-crowdkit")`'s copied-source example. Despite that
shared lineage, they still disagree 121 of the 454 NPI-years where both
are observed (26.6%). The prototype script's response was to treat
agreement as one combined vote and disagreement as *no* vote at all, never
picking one arbitrarily -- independently arriving at exactly
`attribute_truth_fusion()`'s own `on_source_conflict = "single_value"`
policy, in unrelated code written for an unrelated reason.

## A complicated case, with a known answer

Even three real, independent sources and an independent corroboration
signal are not the same as a *known* answer -- `confirmed` is itself a
heuristic, not verified truth, and there is still no reference table to
check any method against (`docs/validation-protocol.md` is why). To see
what it looks like when weighted inference provably outperforms majority
vote, with no ambiguity about which one actually won, this section uses a
constructed scenario instead: 16 physician-years, 5 sources with
deliberately different, realistic reliability profiles, and a ground
truth the sources are measured against -- impossible with real data,
which is exactly why this part is simulated, not real.

```{r complicated-setup}
states <- c("CO", "NM", "TX", "AZ", "UT", "NV", "OR", "WA", "ID", "MT", "WY", "KS", "NE", "SD", "ND", "OK")
true_state <- states # task i's true state is states[i]

# Each source's error pattern across the first 15 tasks is independent of
# the others -- this is what lets Dawid-Skene learn differential source
# reliability at all. Task 16 is a deliberately engineered hard case.
wrong_state_for <- function(i) states[((i + 1) %% length(states)) + 1]
errs <- list(
  nppes_recent         = c(3),                     # wrong on 1/15 -- highly reliable
  pecos                = c(7, 11),                  # wrong on 2/15 -- highly reliable
  state_board          = c(2, 5, 9, 13),            # wrong on 4/15 -- moderate
  specialty_directory  = c(1, 4, 6, 8, 10, 13, 14),  # wrong on 7/15 -- close to chance
  patient_review_site  = c(2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) # wrong on 8/15 -- below chance
)
claims2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:15, function(i) {
  data.frame(
    entity_id = as.character(i), attribute = "practice_state", reference_year = 2026,
    source_id = names(errs),
    claimed_value = vapply(errs, function(e) if (i %in% e) wrong_state_for(i) else true_state[i], character(1))
  )
}))
# Task 16: the 3 least reliable sources happen to agree with each other on
# a WRONG value ("KS"), outvoting the 2 most reliable sources' correct,
# unanimous "OK" -- 3 votes beats 2 under plain majority vote.
claims2 <- rbind(claims2, data.frame(
  entity_id = "16", attribute = "practice_state", reference_year = 2026,
  source_id = names(errs), claimed_value = c("OK", "OK", "KS", "KS", "KS")
))
true_state_by_entity <- stats::setNames(true_state, as.character(1:16))
```

```{r complicated-majority}
majority_result2 <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims2, method = "majority")
majority_correct <- sum(
  majority_result2$predictions$predicted_value ==
    true_state_by_entity[majority_result2$predictions$entity_id],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
sprintf("majority vote: %d/16 correct", majority_correct)
```

```{r complicated-ds, eval = crowdkit_available}
ds_result2 <- suppressWarnings(attribute_truth_fusion(claims2, method = "dawid_skene"))
ds_correct <- sum(
  ds_result2$predictions$predicted_value == true_state_by_entity[ds_result2$predictions$entity_id],
  na.rm = TRUE
)
sprintf("dawid_skene: %d/16 correct", ds_correct)
unique(ds_result2$source_diagnostics[, c("source_id", "reliability_score")])
```

Majority gets 14 of 16 right; `dawid_skene` gets all 16. The two it fixes
are revealing. Task 16 is the one engineered above: `state_board`,
`specialty_directory`, and `patient_review_site` all happen to say `"KS"`
(wrong), outvoting the correct, unanimous `"OK"` from `nppes_recent` and
`pecos` 3 votes to 2 -- majority has no way to know those three votes come from
its *least* reliable sources, so it just counts them. Task 13 breaks the
same way, but it wasn't engineered -- it happened on its own, from the
same three unreliable sources' independently-chosen error tasks
coincidentally landing on task 13 together. `dawid_skene` gets both right
because its learned `reliability_score` (above) correctly ranks
`nppes_recent` and `pecos` well above the other three -- so when they
disagree, their two votes outweigh the other three's three votes, not
the other way around.

This is the genuine, checkable case for the extra complexity: when
several sources are available and their reliabilities actually differ
in a learnable way, weighting votes by *learned* reliability can recover
the right answer even when it is not the plurality. It required five
sources with real, differentiated reliability and a known truth to show
cleanly -- conditions the real midwifery data above does not have, and
most real administrative panels won't either. That gap, not any flaw in
the method, is why `docs/validation-protocol.md` exists: a real benchmark
needs real data with both of those properties, which has not yet been
identified (`docs/validation-protocol.md` §0).

## The actual right tool for this specific disagreement

This dataset's disagreement is, by construction, a **staleness** problem:
one extraction is dated 2017, the other 2026, for the same registry. This
package already has a purpose-built tool for exactly that question, and it
gives a far simpler answer than any of the three fusion methods above:

```{r staleness}
disagreeing <- data.frame(
  entity_id = disagreeing_ids,
  updated_2017 = as.Date("2017-01-01"),
  updated_2026 = as.Date("2026-01-01")
)
disagreeing$which_is_newer <- classify_record_staleness(disagreeing$updated_2017, disagreeing$updated_2026)
table(disagreeing$which_is_newer)
```

Every single disagreement resolves to `"a_predates_b"` -- the 2017
extraction is older than the 2026 one, for all 15, because that is simply
true of the two extraction dates and has nothing to do with per-record
content. For a question dated to 2026, "trust the newer snapshot" is a
far simpler, more defensible answer than anything Dawid-Skene or
TruthFinder computed above, *because the actual disagreement mechanism
here is recency, not differing source reliability*. Reaching for
`attribute_truth_fusion()`'s probabilistic backends on a problem that is
really a staleness problem is reaching for the wrong tool --
`record_age_years()`, `classify_record_staleness()`, and
`attribute_lead_lag_matrix()` (see `vignette("lead-lag-staleness")`) are
built for exactly this question, and answer it without needing to model
source reliability at all.

## What this case study does and does not show

It shows real disagreement rates on two real pipelines -- 10.75% at the
state level across nine years on the two-source NPPES panel, 26.6% between
DAC and PECOS despite a shared upstream dependency on the three-source
cohort -- and real, verified output from all three method families on
both. It shows a real limitation (majority's two-source ceiling: agree or
tie, never actually resolve) and a real caveat that persists even with
three sources and an independent corroboration signal (`dawid_skene`
cannot distinguish "this source is less reliable" from "this source is
simply older," and `confirmed` is a stability heuristic, not verified
truth). It does **not** show which method, or which source, is actually
correct for any of these real NPIs -- no phone-verified or board-verified
reference location exists for either real cohort (see
`docs/validation-protocol.md`), and nothing in this vignette should be
read as a benchmark accuracy result. Adding a third independent source
(done above, with real data) sharpened the comparison -- majority now
abstains less and can be meaningfully resolved rather than only tied -- but
it did not supply a verified answer; only a genuinely independent
reference standard can do that, and building one is exactly what that
protocol is for.
